summary.text: Apply the assumed positivity at a suitably large factorial index to obtain primes \(p=6x-1\) and \(r=6y+1\) with \(p+r=6M!\). If Sophie Germain primes are bounded, then \(p\le M\), while if twin pairs are bounded, then \(r\le M\); in either case the bounded prime divides \(M!\), hence divides the other prime and must equal it, contradicting the strict inequality forced by the large sum \(6M!\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\sum_{1\le x<n} I_n(x),
\]
where, for each such \(x\), we put \(y=n-x\), and where \(I_n(x)=1\) precisely when all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime; otherwise \(I_n(x)=0\). Thus \(A(n)\) is exactly the number of decompositions \(n=x+y\), with \(x,y>0\), for which \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime and \(6y-1,6y+1\) form a twin-prime pair. Indeed,
\[
12x-1=2(6x-1)+1,
\]
so primality of both \(6x-1\) and \(12x-1\) says that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime.

Assume throughout that
\[
A(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We prove separately that the Sophie Germain primes and the twin-prime pairs are infinite.

First observe the immediate consequence of positivity that will be used in both parts. Since every summand \(I_n(x)\) is either \(0\) or \(1\), if \(A(n)>0\), then at least one summand is \(1\). Consequently there is an integer \(x\) satisfying
\[
1\le x<n
\]
such that, on setting \(y=n-x\), all of
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Notice that \(x<n\) implies \(y=n-x>0\).

We will also repeatedly use the following elementary facts about factorials. If \(M\ge 3\), then \(M!\ge M\ge 3\), and hence \(M!>1\). Moreover, every positive integer \(d\le M\) divides \(M!\). Finally, if positive integers \(u,v\) satisfy
\[
u+v=6M!
\]
and \(u\le M\), then \(u<v\). To see this, note that
\[
2u\le 2M<6M\le 6M!=u+v,
\]
so cancellation of \(u\) gives \(u<v\). By the same argument, if \(v\le M\), then \(v<u\).

### Infinitely many Sophie Germain primes

Suppose for contradiction that there are only finitely many Sophie Germain primes. Since a finite set of natural numbers is bounded, there is an integer \(N\) such that every Sophie Germain prime is at most \(N\). Set
\[
M=\max\{N,3\}.
\]
Then \(M\ge3\), \(N\le M\), and \(M!>1\). Apply the assumed positivity to \(n=M!\). By the preceding witness argument, there is an \(x\) with
\[
1\le x<M!
\]
such that, with
\[
y=M!-x,
\]
the four numbers
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime.

Define
\[
p=6x-1,
\qquad
r=6y+1.
\]
The number \(p\) is a Sophie Germain prime: it is prime, and
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1
\]
is also prime. Therefore, by the assumed bound on all Sophie Germain primes,
\[
p\le N\le M.
\]
The number \(r=6y+1\) is prime as well.

Since \(x\ge1\) and \(y=M!-x\), ordinary arithmetic gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
p+r
 &= (6x-1)+(6y+1)\\
 &=6(x+y)\\
 &=6M!.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(p\) is a positive integer and \(p\le M\), it divides \(M!\), and hence it divides \(6M!\). The displayed identity shows that \(p\mid p+r\). Since of course \(p\mid p\), subtraction yields
\[
p\mid r.
\]
But both \(p\) and \(r\) are prime. A prime divisor of a prime must equal that prime, so
\[
p=r.
\]
On the other hand, \(p+r=6M!\), \(p\le M\), and \(M\ge3\). The elementary estimate above therefore gives
\[
p<r,
\]
contradicting \(p=r\). Thus the Sophie Germain primes cannot be bounded, and in particular there are infinitely many of them.

### Infinitely many twin-prime pairs

A twin-prime pair will be represented by its smaller member: thus the relevant set consists of primes \(q\) for which \(q+2\) is also prime. Suppose for contradiction that there are only finitely many such smaller twin primes. Then there is an integer \(N\) such that every prime \(q\) with \(q+2\) prime satisfies
\[
q\le N.
\]
This time set
\[
M=\max\{N+2,3\}.
\]
Then \(M\ge3\), \(N+2\le M\), and again \(M!>1\). Apply the positivity assumption to \(n=M!\). We obtain an integer \(x\) with
\[
1\le x<M!,
\]
and, setting
\[
y=M!-x>0,
\]
we know that
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime.

Define
\[
p=6x-1,
\qquad
q=6y-1,
\qquad
r=6y+1.
\]
Then \(p,q,r\) are prime. Moreover, because \(y>0\), the expressions have their usual integer values and
\[
q+2=(6y-1)+2=6y+1=r.
\]
Thus \(q\) is the smaller member of a twin-prime pair. By the hypothetical bound,
\[
q\le N.
\]
It follows that
\[
r=q+2\le N+2\le M.
\]
As in the first part, the decomposition \(M!=x+y\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
p+r
 &= (6x-1)+(6y+1)\\
 &=6(x+y)\\
 &=6M!.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(r\) is positive and \(r\le M\), it divides \(M!\), hence also \(6M!\). Therefore the identity above implies that \(r\mid p+r\). Since \(r\mid r\), subtraction gives
\[
r\mid p.
\]
Both \(r\) and \(p\) are prime, so this forces
\[
r=p.
\]
Yet \(p+r=6M!\), \(r\le M\), and \(M\ge3\). Applying the elementary factorial estimate with the bounded summand now equal to \(r\), we obtain
\[
r<p,
\]
again a contradiction.

Hence the set of smaller members of twin-prime pairs is unbounded and therefore infinite. Distinct smaller members represent distinct twin-prime pairs, so there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

We have proved that the assumption \(A(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\) implies both infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
